item.title: Salesforce Flow Loop Element Cheat Sheet: Bulk-Safe Collections and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: The Loop element lets a Flow work through a collection one record at a time. Admin II interviews ask about it because loops are where Flows either stay…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
The Loop element lets a Flow work through a collection one record at a time. Admin II interviews ask about it because loops are where Flows either stay bulk-safe or hit governor limits.

The 4 Loop Pieces

Piece What it does Key point
Collection variable Holds the records to process Often from Get Records
Loop element Hands you one item at a time Exposes the current item variable
Assignment inside Changes the current item or builds an output collection No DML here
Data element after Saves the output collection once One Update Records outside the loop

Interview Q&A

1. What does the Loop element do?

It goes through a collection and gives you one item at a time as a loop variable. It has two paths: For Each Item runs for every item, and After Last Item runs once at the end.

Tip: Put the save step on After Last Item.

2. Why not put Update Records inside the loop?

Each pass would run one DML call. With many records you hit governor limits and the Flow fails. Instead, add each changed item to a second collection, then update that collection once after the loop.

Tip: Never put DML or Get Records inside a loop.

3. How do you change a field on the current item?

Use an Assignment inside the loop to set the field on the loop variable, then add the loop variable to an output collection.

Tip: Loop variable in, output collection out.

4. Can you loop in reverse?

Yes. The Loop element has a direction setting: first to last or last to first.

Tip: Use reverse when order matters.

5. When can you skip the loop?

Often a Flow does not need one. Update Records with conditions can change every matching record in a single element, and a before-save flow can set fields on the triggering record directly.

Tip: No loop is the safest loop.

6. How do you debug a loop?

Run Debug and watch the loop variable change on each pass. Use the Flow's fault path and, for large data, test with a small set first.

Tip: Test with 2 records, then 200.

Scenario Question

"Set every open Opportunity on an Account to Needs Review when the Account is marked At Risk."

  1. Record-triggered flow on Account, after save, when At_Risk__c becomes true
  2. Get Records: open Opportunities where AccountId equals the Account Id
  3. Loop through them, with an Assignment setting StageName and adding each to an output collection
  4. Update Records on the output collection, once, after the loop

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add Get Records for a few Contacts into a collection.
  2. Add a Loop over that collection.
  3. Inside the loop, add an Assignment that sets the current Contact's Description, then adds it to a new collection.
  4. After the last item, add Update Records using the new collection.
  5. Run Debug and check the Contacts in your org.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Loop = one item at a time
  • For Each Item = runs per record
  • After Last Item = runs once at the end
  • Output collection = what you save
  • DML = outside the loop
  • Often no loop = Update Records with conditions

Key Takeaways

  • Loop through a collection, build an output collection, save once.
  • Never put DML or Get Records inside a loop.
  • Skip the loop when one element can do the job.
  • Test with small data first.

Next up: Flow formulas and how they replace small pieces of logic.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Do you try to avoid loops, or use them often? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS CloudWatch Basics: Metrics, Logs and Alarms for Your Resources
item.description: Last time I looked at who changed things with CloudTrail. The next question is different: what is happening inside my resources right now? That is Amazon…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Last time I looked at who changed things with CloudTrail. The next question is different: what is happening inside my resources right now? That is Amazon CloudWatch.

What CloudWatch does

  • Metrics: numbers over time, such as EC2 CPU utilization or S3 request counts.
  • Logs: log data from your applications and services, stored in log groups.
  • Alarms: watch a metric and do something when it crosses a threshold.
  • Dashboards: put the graphs you care about on one page.

CloudTrail vs CloudWatch

Question Service
Who made this change? CloudTrail
Is this resource healthy and busy? CloudWatch

How an alarm works

  • An alarm watches one metric over a period (for example, 5 minutes).
  • Its state is OK, ALARM or INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
  • When the state changes, it can send a message to an SNS topic, which can email you.
  • The threshold and the number of periods to evaluate decide how sensitive it is.

Good to know

  • EC2 sends basic metrics every 5 minutes by default, and detailed monitoring gives 1-minute data (extra cost).
  • EC2 does not report memory or disk usage by default. You need the CloudWatch agent for those.
  • Logs stay forever unless you set a retention period, so set one.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open CloudWatch and browse All metrics for EC2 or S3.
  2. Choose Alarms, then Create alarm.
  3. Pick a metric, such as EC2 CPUUtilization for one instance.
  4. Set a threshold, for example greater than 70% for 2 periods.
  5. Create or choose an SNS topic with your email, and confirm the subscription email.
  6. Save the alarm and check that it shows OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA at first.

Common mistakes

  • Creating alarms with no action, so nobody is told.
  • Forgetting to confirm the SNS email subscription.
  • Expecting memory metrics without the CloudWatch agent.
  • Leaving log groups on never-expire retention.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail tells you who changed it, CloudWatch tells you how it is doing.
  • Metrics feed alarms, alarms feed SNS, SNS reaches you.
  • Install the agent for memory and disk.
  • Set log retention.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to use tags to keep resources organized and costs traceable.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Create, Update and Delete Records Cheat Sheet: Fault Paths and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Create Records, Update Records and Delete Records are how a Flow changes data. Admin II interviews ask about them because small choices here decide whether…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Create Records, Update Records and Delete Records are how a Flow changes data. Admin II interviews ask about them because small choices here decide whether a Flow is safe, fast and bulk-ready.

The 3 Data Elements

Element What it does Key point
Create Records Adds new records Can store the new record Id
Update Records Changes existing records Filter, or pass a record or collection
Delete Records Removes records Use filters or a collection, and be careful

Interview Q&A

1. How does Create Records set field values?

Either set the fields one by one, or use all values from a record variable or collection you built earlier. Choose Create multiple records when you pass a collection.

Tip: Build a collection, then create once.

2. How can Update Records pick what to change?

Two ways: specify conditions and set fields individually, or use the Ids and all field values from a record or collection. The first changes every record that matches the filter.

Tip: Check the filter before you run it.

3. Why store the new record Id?

After Create Records you can store the Id in a variable. Use it to create related records, such as a Task linked to the new Case.

Tip: Store the Id, then relate children to it.

4. How do you make a Flow bulk-safe?

Do the work on a collection: add records to it in the loop with an Assignment, and run one Create, Update or Delete Records after the loop.

Tip: DML belongs outside the loop.

5. What is a fault path?

A fault connector that runs when a data element fails, for example on a validation rule error. Use it to show a message or log the error.

Tip: Add a fault path to every data element.

6. Update Records or an Assignment on $Record?

In a before-save record-triggered flow, an Assignment on $Record changes the record with no extra DML. In an after-save flow, use Update Records to change the triggering record or related records.

Tip: Before-save is faster for same-record updates.

Scenario Question

"When a Case is closed, create a follow-up Task and mark the related Contact as contacted."

  1. Record-triggered flow on Case, after save, when Status changes to Closed
  2. Create Records: a Task, with WhatId set to the Case Id
  3. Update Records: set the Contact's Last_Contacted__c field
  4. Fault path on both elements, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a text input for a Case subject.
  2. Add Create Records for Case, set Subject from the input, and store the new Id in a variable.
  3. Add Update Records that sets the same Case's Priority to High using that Id.
  4. Add a fault path from each element to a screen that shows {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.
  5. Run Debug and check the new Case in your org.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Add = Create Records
  • Change = Update Records
  • Remove = Delete Records
  • Many at once = collection, one element after the loop
  • Failure = fault path
  • Same record, before save = Assignment on $Record

Key Takeaways

  • Work on collections, then save once.
  • Store the Id to build related records.
  • Add a fault path to every data element.
  • Be careful with filters on Update and Delete.

Next up: the Loop element and how to process collections safely.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which data element do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS CloudTrail Basics: Who Did What, When and From Where
item.description: This week I locked the root account and set a budget. Now the question that comes after both: when something changes in the account, how do I find out who…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
This week I locked the root account and set a budget. Now the question that comes after both: when something changes in the account, how do I find out who did it, what they did and when? That is AWS CloudTrail.

What CloudTrail records

  • CloudTrail logs API activity in your account, whether it came from the console, the CLI, an SDK or another AWS service.
  • Each event says who (the identity), what (the API call), when, and where from (the source IP address).
  • It is the audit trail you open when a resource disappears or a setting changes.

Event types

Type What it covers Notes
Management events Control-plane actions, such as creating a role or launching an instance Recorded by default
Data events Object-level actions, such as S3 object reads or Lambda invokes Off by default, extra cost
Insights events Unusual API activity Optional

Event history vs a trail

  • Event history is on by default and lets you look up recent management events (the last 90 days) in the console, with no setup.
  • A trail delivers events to an S3 bucket (and optionally CloudWatch Logs) so you keep them longer and can search them with other tools.
  • A multi-Region trail records activity in all Regions, so nothing slips through in a Region you do not use.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open CloudTrail and choose Event history.
  2. Filter by Event name ConsoleLogin and open one event to see who signed in and from which IP address.
  3. Filter by User name root to check whether root has been used, tying back to the root account checklist.
  4. Choose Create trail, name it, and create or choose an S3 bucket for the logs.
  5. Enable a multi-Region trail and log file validation, then create it.
  6. After a few minutes, open the S3 bucket and find the delivered log files.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on event history only, then needing events older than 90 days.
  • Creating a trail in one Region and missing activity elsewhere.
  • Leaving the log bucket open. Keep it private.
  • Turning on data events everywhere without checking the cost.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail answers who, what, when and from where.
  • Event history is free to browse, a trail keeps the records.
  • Use a multi-Region trail and keep the bucket private.
  • Check root activity regularly.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see what is happening inside your resources, not just who changed them.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Get Records Cheat Sheet: Filters, Sort Order, Null Checks and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Get Records is how a Flow reads data. Admin II interviews ask about its filters, sort order and null checks because a badly built one is the most common…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Get Records is how a Flow reads data. Admin II interviews ask about its filters, sort order and null checks because a badly built one is the most common cause of slow or broken Flows.

The 4 Settings That Matter

Setting What it controls Key point
Filter conditions Which records come back AND, OR or custom logic
Sort order Which record is "first" Set it whenever you need one record
How many records One or many Only the first record, or all records
Store fields What data is kept Choose only the fields you need

Interview Q&A

1. How do you filter a Get Records?

Add filter conditions on the object's fields, such as Status Equals Open. Combine them with All Conditions Are Met (AND), Any Condition Is Met (OR) or Custom Condition Logic.

Tip: Filter in Get Records, not after it.

2. Why does sort order matter?

With Only the first record, Salesforce returns the first match in your sort order. Without a sort, which record you get is not guaranteed.

Tip: Sort by CreatedDate descending for "latest".

3. One record or all records?

Only the first record stores a single record variable. All records stores a collection you can loop over.

Tip: Match the choice to the variable you need.

4. Which fields should you store?

Choose only the fields you need instead of all fields. Fewer fields means less data to carry through the Flow.

Tip: Name the fields you will actually read.

5. What if no record is found?

The variable is empty (null). Add a Decision after the Get Records that checks whether the variable Is Null, and handle that path.

Tip: Always plan the "found nothing" path.

6. Why keep Get Records out of loops?

Each Get Records is a SOQL query, and a transaction has a limit on queries. A query inside a loop can hit that limit on bulk data.

Tip: Query once before the loop, then loop the collection.

Scenario Question

"A flow must find the most recent open Case for a Contact and show its subject."

  1. Get Records on Case: ContactId Equals the Contact AND Status Does Not Equal Closed
  2. Sort by CreatedDate descending, Only the first record
  3. Decision: is the Case variable Is Null?
  4. Display the Subject, or a "No open cases" message

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add a Get Records element on Case, returning Only the first record.
  2. Add a filter Status Does Not Equal Closed and sort by CreatedDate descending.
  3. Choose Choose fields and let Salesforce do the rest and pick Subject and Status.
  4. Add a Decision that checks the Case variable Is Null and a screen for each path.
  5. Run Debug with a Contact who has open cases and one who has none.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Read data = Get Records
  • Narrow it down = filter conditions
  • Pick the first = sort order
  • A list = All records (collection)
  • Nothing found = Is Null Decision
  • Efficiency = store only needed fields, no queries in loops

Key Takeaways

  • Filter and sort inside Get Records.
  • Always handle the nothing-found path.
  • Store only the fields you need.
  • Query once, then loop.

Next up: Update Records and Create Records, and how they save changes.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which Get Records setting trips you up? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Budgets and Billing Alerts: Set a Spending Limit Before You Build
item.description: Yesterday I locked down the root account and noted "keep billing alerts up to date". Today is the other half of the front door: making sure a forgotten…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I locked down the root account and noted "keep billing alerts up to date". Today is the other half of the front door: making sure a forgotten resource never turns into a surprise bill. AWS Budgets does that.

What AWS Budgets does

  • You set a spending limit (or a usage limit) and AWS compares your actual and forecasted spend against it.
  • When a threshold is crossed, it emails you (and can notify an SNS topic).
  • Spend data is not instant. Billing data can lag, so treat alerts as an early warning, not a live meter.

Types of budget

Type Tracks Good for
Cost budget Dollars spent Almost every learner
Usage budget Units used, such as hours or GB Watching a specific service
Savings Plans / Reservation budgets Coverage and utilization Later, when you commit to spend

Two templates to start with

  • Zero spend budget: alerts you as soon as your spend goes above the free tier. Ideal for a learning account.
  • Monthly cost budget: you choose a monthly amount, and the console sets alerts at 85% of actual spend, 100% of actual spend and 100% of forecasted spend.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Sign in and open Billing and Cost Management, then Budgets.
  2. Choose Create budget and pick a template, such as Zero spend budget or Monthly cost budget.
  3. Name it, set the amount (for example 10 USD) and add the email addresses to alert.
  4. Review the thresholds and create the budget.
  5. Optionally, as the root user, turn on IAM user and role access to Billing information so your admin identity can see costs without using root.

Common mistakes

  • Creating a budget but typing the email address wrongly.
  • Setting only an actual-spend alert, so you hear about a problem after the money is gone.
  • Forgetting that some services keep charging until you delete the resource.
  • Using root every time to check the bill instead of enabling billing access for IAM.

Worth knowing next

Cost Explorer shows where your spend comes from, and Cost Anomaly Detection can flag unusual spikes. Budgets tells you that spend is rising. Those two help explain why.

Key takeaways

  • Create a budget before you create any real resources.
  • Alert on forecasted spend as well as actual spend.
  • Give billing access to an IAM admin, not just root.
  • Delete what you stop using.

Tomorrow I'll go one step further into securing access to the account.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Decision and Assignment Elements Cheat Sheet: Outcomes, Operators and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Decisions send a flow down the right path. Assignments change values along the way. Admin II interviews ask about both because almost every real Flow uses…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Decisions send a flow down the right path. Assignments change values along the way. Admin II interviews ask about both because almost every real Flow uses them.

The 2 Elements

Element What it does Key point
Decision Routes the flow into one path Outcomes are checked top to bottom, the first match wins
Assignment Sets or changes values Changes variables, not the database

Interview Q&A

1. How does a Decision pick a path?

It checks its outcomes from top to bottom. The first outcome whose conditions are met runs. If none match, the Default Outcome runs.

Tip: Put the most specific outcome first.

2. How can outcome conditions be combined?

Choose All Conditions Are Met (AND), Any Condition Is Met (OR), Custom Logic such as 1 AND (2 OR 3), or Always (No Conditions Required).

Tip: Use custom logic for mixed AND and OR.

3. What does an Assignment do?

It sets values on variables, including fields of a record variable such as {!caseRecord.Status}. Operators include Equals, Add and Subtract.

Tip: Equals overwrites, Add accumulates.

4. Does an Assignment save to the database?

No. It only changes values in the flow. Use Update Records to save, except for $Record in a before-save record-triggered flow, which saves automatically.

Tip: Assignment edits, Update Records saves.

5. How do you build up a collection?

Use an Assignment on a collection variable with the Add operator to put each record in the list. Then use one Update Records after the loop.

Tip: Never put DML inside a loop.

6. What should the Default Outcome do?

Handle everything no outcome matched. Rename it so the path is clear, and leave it connected to something, even a simple end.

Tip: Plan the "none of the above" case.

Scenario Question

"A record-triggered flow must escalate high-priority Cases from Premium accounts."

  1. Decision: Priority equals High AND account type is Premium
  2. Assignment: set Escalated to true and Status to Escalated on {!caseRecord}
  3. Assignment: add the record to a collection
  4. One Update Records after the loop, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a Get Records for one Case into a record variable.
  2. Add a Decision with an outcome High Priority where Priority equals High, and leave the Default Outcome as Other.
  3. On the High Priority path, add an Assignment that sets {!caseRecord.Status} to Escalated.
  4. Add an Update Records element that saves {!caseRecord}.
  5. Run Debug with a High priority Case and then a Low priority Case, and compare the paths.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Choose a path = Decision
  • Change a value = Assignment
  • Order of outcomes = top to bottom
  • None matched = Default Outcome
  • Save changes = Update Records
  • Add to a list = Assignment on a collection

Key Takeaways

  • Decisions route, Assignments change values.
  • The first matching outcome wins.
  • Assignments do not save to the database.
  • Keep DML outside loops.

Next up: the Get Records element and how filters and sort order work.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which element do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: Protect the AWS Root Account and Turn on MFA
item.description: Every AWS account starts with one identity that can do everything: the root user. IAM policies cannot restrict it, so if someone gets in, there is no…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every AWS account starts with one identity that can do everything: the root user. IAM policies cannot restrict it, so if someone gets in, there is no safety net. Before building anything else, lock it down.

What the root user is (and is not)

  • It is the email address you signed up with, and it has unrestricted access to the whole account, including billing and closing the account.
  • It is not an IAM user, so you cannot limit it with a policy.
  • You should almost never sign in with it. Daily work belongs to IAM identities (Day 1) and roles (Day 3).

The root account checklist

Step Why it matters
Turn on MFA for the root user A stolen password alone is no longer enough
Use a long, unique password in a password manager Root should not share a password with anything else
Delete root access keys (or never create them) A leaked key would have full power with no MFA prompt
Use a shared mailbox or alias you control You keep recovery access if one person leaves
Keep alternate contacts and billing alerts up to date You hear about problems early

Choosing an MFA type

  • Passkey or security key (FIDO2): phishing-resistant, the strongest everyday option.
  • Authenticator app (TOTP): free, quick to set up, and fine for most learners.
  • Hardware TOTP token: a physical code generator, mostly for strict environments.

You can register more than one MFA device on the same user, so add a second one as a backup.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Sign in as the root user, open the account menu and choose Security credentials.
  2. Under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), choose Assign MFA device.
  3. Give it a clear name, pick Authenticator app or Passkey or security key, and follow the prompts.
  4. Under Access keys, confirm there are none. If there are, delete them.
  5. Sign out and sign in again to confirm the MFA prompt appears.
  6. Create an IAM admin identity for daily use and stop using root.

Common mistakes

  • Using root for everyday tasks "just this once".
  • Keeping root access keys in a script or a laptop folder.
  • Registering MFA on a single phone with no backup device.
  • Using a personal inbox that only one person can read.

What only root can do

A short list of tasks still needs root, such as changing the account name or email, closing the account and restoring IAM permissions if you lock yourself out. That is the only reason to sign in as root.

Key takeaways

  • The root user is unrestricted, so protect it before anything else.
  • Turn on MFA, remove access keys and keep a backup MFA device.
  • Do real work with IAM users and roles, not root.

Tomorrow I'll look at what comes next once the front door is locked.

item.title: IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials for EC2
item.description: On Day 2 I wrote a least-privilege policy for one S3 bucket. The next question is who gets to use it. For people, that's a user or group. For servers and…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
On Day 2 I wrote a least-privilege policy for one S3 bucket. The next question is who gets to use it. For people, that's a user or group. For servers and apps, it should be a role, so nothing long-lived ever sits on the machine.

Users vs roles

IAM user IAM role
For A person A service, an app or a person who needs temporary access
Credentials Long-term (password, access keys) Temporary, issued on demand
Rotation You do it Automatic
Typical use Console and CLI sign-in EC2, Lambda, cross-account access

Two policies on every role

  • Trust policy: who is allowed to assume the role (for example ec2.amazonaws.com).
  • Permissions policy: what the role can do once assumed (for example the Day 2 S3 read policy).

A trust policy for EC2 looks like this:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

How EC2 gets credentials

  1. The role is attached to the instance through an instance profile (the console creates it for you when you make an EC2 role).
  2. Software on the instance asks the instance metadata service for credentials.
  3. STS (Security Token Service) issues a temporary access key, secret key and session token.
  4. AWS refreshes them automatically before they expire, so nothing is stored on disk.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Create a role: trusted entity AWS service, EC2.
  2. Attach the ReadDemoBucketOnly policy from Day 2 (or any least-privilege S3 read policy).
  3. Launch a small EC2 instance and attach the role under Actions, Security, Modify IAM role.
  4. Connect to the instance and run:
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws s3 ls s3://your-demo-bucket
aws s3 ls s3://some-other-bucket   # should be denied
  1. To see the temporary credentials the instance receives (IMDSv2):
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600")
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/

get-caller-identity should show an assumed-role ARN instead of a user, which proves the instance is using the role. Don't paste the credentials from the metadata call anywhere.

Common mistakes to avoid

  1. Putting access keys in code, config files or an AMI "just for now".
  2. Making the trust policy too wide, for example trusting a whole account when one role is enough.
  3. Attaching AdministratorAccess to a role so the app "just works".
  4. Forgetting the role is attached to the instance but the app still uses old keys from a config file.

3 habits I'm keeping

  1. Workloads get roles, people get users or federated sign-in, never the other way round.
  2. Keep trust and permissions separate and check both when access fails.
  3. Run aws sts get-caller-identity first whenever something is denied.

Tomorrow (Day 4): protecting the root account and turning on MFA.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Variables & Resources Cheat Sheet: Constants, Formulas, Collections and Admin II Interview Q&A (Day 1/120)
item.description: Variables, constants, formulas and collections are the building blocks of every Flow. Admin II interviews ask about them to see if you can build, not just…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Variables, constants, formulas and collections are the building blocks of every Flow. Admin II interviews ask about them to see if you can build, not just click.

The 4 Building Blocks

Resource What it holds Key point
Variable A value Changes via Assignment
Constant A fixed value Never changes
Formula A calculated value Read-only, calculated live
Collection A list of values or records Allow multiple values

Interview Q&A

1. Variable, Constant or Formula?

Variables change through Assignment. Constants never change. Formulas calculate when they are used.

Tip: Need to change it? Use a variable.

2. What is a record variable?

One variable that holds a whole record. Read its fields as {!recVar.Field}.

Tip: Fill it with Get Records.

3. What is a collection variable?

A variable with Allow multiple values turned on. It holds a list you can loop over.

Tip: Name it plural, like contactList.

4. What do the input and output settings do?

Input lets a caller pass values in (a subflow, Apex or a URL). Output returns values to the caller.

Tip: Open only what you need.

5. What is $Record?

The record that triggered a record-triggered flow. $Record__Prior holds the old values on updates.

Tip: Compare old to new.

6. Text Template or Formula?

Text Template builds readable text with merge fields. A Formula returns a calculated value.

Tip: Emails and screen messages: use a template.

Scenario Question

"A screen flow must show a 10% discount on an Opportunity."

  1. Get Records into an Opportunity variable
  2. Formula: Amount x 0.1
  3. Text Template: build the message
  4. Show it on a screen, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add a Get Records element for one Opportunity into a record variable.
  2. Add a Formula resource of type Currency: {!oppRecord.Amount} * 0.1.
  3. Add a Text Template that says "Discount: {!discountFormula}".
  4. Show the template in a Display Text component on a screen.
  5. Run Debug and check the value against the Opportunity amount.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Change = variable
  • Fixed = constant
  • Calculate = formula
  • Message = text template
  • List = collection
  • Trigger record = $Record

Key Takeaways

  • Pick the right resource type.
  • Use a Formula for any calculation.
  • Open input and output with care.
  • Name every resource clearly.

item.title: Salesforce Admin Interview Final Checklist: Security, Automation, Data, and Scenario Answers (Day 30/30)
item.description: 30 days, 30 topics, one cheat sheet to finish. This is the checklist I would run through before any Salesforce admin interview. Start with OWD, then open…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
30 days, 30 topics, one cheat sheet to finish. This is the checklist I would run through before any Salesforce admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Security OWD, roles, sharing Open up access
Automation Flow and approvals Lightest tool
Data Import, clean, back up Prevent first
Delivery Sandbox to production Test first

Interview Q&A

1. Where do you start on access?

Start with OWD, then open up with roles, sharing rules and permission sets.

Tip: Open up, never lock down.

2. Flow or validation rule?

Validation blocks bad data. Flow automates the actions.

Tip: Use the lightest tool.

3. How do you ship changes?

Build in a sandbox, then deploy with change sets.

Tip: Test before production.

4. How do you keep data clean?

Use duplicate rules, restricted picklists and validation rules.

Tip: Prevent first, then clean.

5. How do you protect data?

Schedule data exports and know what the Recycle Bin keeps.

Tip: Back up before big changes.

6. How do you answer scenarios?

State the goal, name the tool, give the steps, mention a test.

Tip: Keep it under a minute.

Scenario Question

"A new sales team joins. What do you set up?"

  1. Add roles and permission sets
  2. Set record types and layouts
  3. Build flows and validations
  4. Test in a sandbox first

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Access = OWD first
  • Rules = validation blocks
  • Automation = Flow
  • Release = sandbox first
  • Data = prevent duplicates
  • Answer = goal, tool, steps

Key Takeaways

  • Start with the goal
  • Use the lightest tool
  • Test before production
  • Explain it in four steps

item.title: Salesforce Files & Attachments Cheat Sheet: Libraries, Sharing, Versions, and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 29/30)

item.content:encoded:
Store it once, share it safely, keep every version. Files and attachments come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Files Modern and versioned Up to 2 GB
Attachments Legacy and basic Up to 25 MB
Libraries Shared team folders Member roles
Sharing Links to records Viewer or Collab

Interview Q&A

1. Files or Attachments?

Files are modern: versions, sharing and preview.

Tip: Migrate old attachments.

2. What are the size limits?

Up to 2 GB per file. Legacy attachments allow 25 MB.

Tip: Check your org limits.

3. How are files shared?

Through links to records, people, groups or libraries.

Tip: One file, many records.

4. Viewer or Collaborator?

Viewer can view and download. Collaborator can also edit.

Tip: Default to Viewer.

5. What is a library?

A shared folder for files, with member roles and permissions.

Tip: Use it for team content.

6. Uploading a new version?

The file keeps its history and the same links.

Tip: No need to re-share.

Scenario Question

"Reps must attach signed contracts to Opportunities. How?"

  1. Add Files to the page layout
  2. Store contracts in a library
  3. Set members to Viewer
  4. Test upload and preview

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Files = modern
  • Attachments = legacy
  • Limit = 2 GB per file
  • Share = record links
  • Viewer = view only
  • Version = keeps history

Key Takeaways

  • Use Files, not Attachments
  • Share through records and libraries
  • Give Viewer unless edit is needed
  • Upload versions, do not duplicate

item.title: Salesforce Picklists & Global Value Sets Cheat Sheet: Dependencies, Restrictions, and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 28/30)
item.description: One clean list of values, used everywhere. Picklists, global value sets and dependencies come up in almost every admin interview. A shared list of values…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
One clean list of values, used everywhere. Picklists, global value sets and dependencies come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Picklist One value from a list Admin controlled
Value Set Shared by many fields Edit it once
Dependent Values follow a field Needs a controller
Restricted Blocks unlisted values Cleaner data

Interview Q&A

1. What is a global value set?

A shared list of values reused by many picklists.

Tip: Edit once, update everywhere.

2. What is a dependent picklist?

Its values change based on a controlling field.

Tip: Plan the mapping first.

3. What can be a controller?

A standard or custom picklist, or a checkbox.

Tip: Multi-select cannot control.

4. What does Restrict do?

It blocks values outside the list, even through the API.

Tip: Turn it on for clean data.

5. How do record types help?

Each record type can show only a subset of values.

Tip: Set it per record type.

6. Retiring a value?

Existing records keep it, new records cannot use it.

Tip: Deactivate, do not delete.

Scenario Question

"Sales and Support need the same Region list. How?"

  1. Create a global value set
  2. Attach it to both fields
  3. Restrict the picklist
  4. Limit values per record type

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Shared = global value set
  • Depends = controlling field
  • Controller = picklist or checkbox
  • Restrict = blocks new values
  • Subset = record types
  • Retire = deactivate

Key Takeaways

  • Reuse lists with global value sets
  • Pick the controlling field first
  • Restrict to keep data clean
  • Deactivate instead of deleting

Which picklist is hardest to maintain? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Case Escalation & Entitlements Cheat Sheet: Milestones, Business Hours, and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 27/30)
item.description: Make sure no customer waits longer than promised. Escalation rules and entitlements come up in almost every Service Cloud admin interview. It reassigns or…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Make sure no customer waits longer than promised. Escalation rules and entitlements come up in almost every Service Cloud admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Escalation Acts on open cases One active rule
Business Hours Working time clock Set them first
Entitlement Support level owed Link to account
Milestone Timed required step Warn and violate

Interview Q&A

1. What is an escalation rule?

It reassigns or notifies when a case stays open too long.

Tip: Built for missed deadlines.

2. Assignment or escalation?

Assignment routes new cases. Escalation acts on open ones.

Tip: They work together.

3. How many can be active?

Only one escalation rule is active at a time.

Tip: Use rule entries for variety.

4. Why set business hours?

Timers can count only working hours.

Tip: Add holidays too.

5. What is an entitlement?

It defines the support a customer is owed, like response time.

Tip: Link it to the account.

6. What is a milestone?

A required step with a time limit, such as first response.

Tip: Add warning and violation actions.

Scenario Question

"Premium cases need a reply within an hour. How?"

  1. Create a Premium entitlement
  2. Add a first response milestone
  3. Set warning and violation actions
  4. Test with a sample case

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Assign = routes new cases
  • Escalate = acts on open cases
  • Active = one rule
  • Clock = business hours
  • Entitlement = support level
  • Milestone = time target

Key Takeaways

  • Assign first, escalate later
  • Set business hours before timers
  • Link entitlements to accounts
  • Warn before the violation

Prove who changed what, and when. Field History and the audit trails come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Field History Old and new values 20 fields each
Setup Trail Logs admin changes Last 180 days
Field Audit Paid long retention Up to 10 years
Login History Who logged in Last 6 months

Interview Q&A

1. What is Field History?

It records the old and new values of selected fields.

Tip: Turn it on per object.

2. How many fields can you track?

Up to 20 fields on each object.

Tip: Pick fields that matter.

3. How long is history kept?

18 months in the UI and 24 months through the API.

Tip: Export what you must keep.

4. What is Setup Audit Trail?

It logs setup changes and who made them for 180 days.

Tip: Download the CSV to keep it.

5. Need longer retention?

Field Audit Trail is an add-on: up to 60 fields and 10 years.

Tip: Ask about licensing.

6. Which fields cannot be tracked?

Formula and roll-up summary fields.

Tip: Track the source fields.

Scenario Question

"Auditors ask who changed Amount, and when. How?"

  1. Enable history on Opportunity
  2. Select the Amount field
  3. Show the History related list
  4. Check Setup Audit Trail

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Fields = 20 per object
  • UI = 18 months
  • API = 24 months
  • Setup trail = 180 days
  • Add-on = 60 fields
  • Formulas = not tracked

Key Takeaways

  • Track only fields that matter
  • Export before data ages out
  • Setup Audit Trail covers admin changes
  • Use Field Audit Trail for compliance

item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every support email, tracked as a case from the first message. Email-to-Case comes up in almost every Service Cloud and admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Routing Address Address makes cases Verify it first
On-Demand Salesforce hosts it No agent needed
Standard Agent on your server Behind firewall
Threading Ref ID links replies One case thread

Interview Q&A

1. What is Email-to-Case?

Customer emails automatically become cases in Salesforce.

Tip: No manual typing.

2. On-Demand or Standard?

On-Demand needs no agent. Standard runs an agent behind your firewall.

Tip: Default to On-Demand.

3. What is a routing address?

It links an email address to case settings like origin and priority.

Tip: Verify it before use.

4. How do replies stay on one case?

A Ref ID in the email ties each reply to the same case.

Tip: Keep it in the subject.

5. How do cases get an owner?

Assignment rules route them, or the routing address owner takes them.

Tip: Queues work well.

6. Can customers get a reply?

Yes, auto-response rules confirm the case by email.

Tip: Include the case number.

Scenario Question

"Support inbox emails must become cases. How?"

  1. Enable Email-to-Case in Setup
  2. Create and verify a routing address
  3. Set assignment and auto-response
  4. Test by emailing the inbox

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Email = becomes a case
  • Default = On-Demand
  • Agent = Standard only
  • Address = verify first
  • Thread = Ref ID
  • Reply = auto-response

Key Takeaways

  • Pick On-Demand unless a firewall blocks it
  • Verify every routing address
  • Keep the Ref ID for threading
  • Test with a real email

item.title: My First Hands-On DevOps Lab: Learning Linux, Git, and GitHub from Scratch
item.description: When I started learning DevOps, I wanted to understand everything together: Linux, Git, cloud infrastructure, automation, containers, and deployments. But…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
When I started learning DevOps, I wanted to understand everything together: Linux, Git, cloud infrastructure, automation, containers, and deployments. But I also wanted to understand every command I typed.

So I began with a small hands-on lab on an Ubuntu server. My starting point was a directory called devops-lab and a terminal.

This article captures the foundation: navigating Linux, working with files, and understanding how changes move from a local Git repository to GitHub. The commands below form a simple practice exercise you can adapt to your own lab.

Why start with a small lab?

A deployment pipeline eventually runs commands on a machine, reads files, and works with a version of your code. Learning those basics makes the larger workflow easier to understand.

My goal at this stage is to explain what a command does, run it, inspect the result, and repeat it without blindly copying instructions.

1. Know where you are

In my Ubuntu lab, I started by checking my current directory:

pwd

The output was:

/home/ubuntu/devops-lab

pwd means print working directory. It tells you where commands will operate unless you supply another path.

To create a similar workspace from your home directory:

mkdir -p ~/devops-lab
cd ~/devops-lab
pwd

Here is what each command does:

  • mkdir -p creates the directory if it does not already exist.
  • ~ refers to your user's home directory.
  • cd changes your current directory.
  • pwd confirms your location.

That final check is useful. Before creating or editing files, I want to know exactly where I am.

2. Create a file and inspect it

For a small practice example, create a README:

printf '# My DevOps Lab\n\nLearning Linux and Git through practice.\n' > README.md
cat README.md
ls -l

printf writes the text, while > redirects that output into a file. Be careful: > replaces an existing file's contents.

cat displays the file, and ls -l lists directory contents with details such as permissions, owner, and size.

To add another line without replacing the file:

printf '\nFirst topic: Linux and Git fundamentals.\n' >> README.md
cat README.md

The difference between > and >> is small to type but important to understand: one replaces content; the other appends it.

3. Start tracking the project with Git

Git records versions of a project's tracked files. GitHub hosts repositories remotely so they can be shared and used for collaboration.

From inside the practice directory:

git init
git status

git init creates a Git repository in the directory. It does not upload anything to GitHub.

git status shows the repository's current state. At this point, a new README will normally appear as an untracked file.

Before creating your first commit, configure your commit identity if you have not already done so:

git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "YOUR_GITHUB_NOREPLY_EMAIL"

Replace those values with your own details. You can use the no-reply address provided in your GitHub email settings.

These commands set the identity for this repository. They do not sign you in to GitHub.

4. Understand staging and committing

This was one of the most useful distinctions for me.

A file can exist in my project without being included in the next commit. Staging lets me choose which changes to record.

git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add initial DevOps lab notes"
git status

The sequence matters:

  1. git add README.md stages the file's current contents.
  2. git diff --staged lets me review what the next commit will contain.
  3. git commit records the staged changes in the local repository.
  4. git status shows whether any changes remain.

If I edit the file again after staging it, I need to stage the new changes too if I want them in that commit.

A commit message should explain the change. “Add initial DevOps lab notes” tells me more than “update.”

5. Connect the local repository to GitHub

For this practice workflow, first create an empty GitHub repository, without adding a README, license, or .gitignore through GitHub. That keeps the initial push straightforward.

Then replace the placeholder URL below with your repository URL:

git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPOSITORY.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main

Here is what these commands mean:

Command Purpose
git branch -M main Rename the current branch to main
git remote add origin ... Store the remote repository URL under the name origin
git remote -v Show the configured remote URLs
git push -u origin main Push the branch and set its upstream tracking relationship

Authentication must be configured separately. Use a supported GitHub authentication method, such as an HTTPS credential manager or SSH. Never put tokens or private keys in your project files.

If origin already exists, inspect it with git remote -v before changing anything. If the remote repository already contains commits, its history may need to be integrated before you can push.

6. The difference between commit and push

My simplest explanation is:

A commit records staged changes locally. A push sends local commits to a remote repository.

That means a successful commit does not automatically update GitHub.

For another practice change:

printf '\nKey lesson: commit is local; push updates the remote.\n' >> README.md
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Document the difference between commit and push"
git push

After the upstream is configured, git push can usually use that tracking relationship without repeating the remote and branch names.

The workflow is:

Edit → Review → Stage → Review staged changes → Commit → Push

7. Verify the result

A command finishing without an obvious error is a starting point. I also want to check the result.

git status
git log --oneline -5
git remote -v

These checks answer different questions:

  • Status: Do I have uncommitted changes?
  • Log: Which commits exist locally?
  • Remote: Which repository am I connected to?

Finally, open the repository on GitHub and check that the expected file and latest commit appear.

A clean working tree means there are no outstanding changes relative to the current commit. By itself, it does not prove that every commit has been pushed.

What this lab is teaching me

The biggest lesson is to connect every action with its purpose.

Before running a command, I try to answer:

  • Where am I running it?
  • What will it change?
  • How will I verify the result?
  • What does the output tell me?

I also want to build good habits early: review changes before committing, write useful commit messages, and keep credentials out of version control.

A README is a useful place to record the lab's purpose, commands, results, and lessons. That makes it easier to return later and explain what I actually learned.

What comes next

My next goal is to build on this foundation with a small application, then gradually introduce a web server, scripting, containers, and a CI/CD pipeline.

For this stage, the milestone is clear: work confidently in a Linux directory, inspect a file change, record it with Git, and understand how that commit reaches GitHub.

I am documenting the process as I learn, one practical step at a time.

item.title: Writing a Custom IAM Policy from Scratch
item.description: On Day 1 I used an AWS managed policy (ReadOnlyAccess). It works, but it's broad. Today I wrote my own policy that allows exactly one thing: reading one S3…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
On Day 1 I used an AWS managed policy (ReadOnlyAccess). It works, but it's broad. Today I wrote my own policy that allows exactly one thing: reading one S3 bucket and nothing else. That's least privilege in practice.

Anatomy of an IAM policy

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ReadOneBucketOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::robin-120days-demo",
        "arn:aws:s3:::robin-120days-demo/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
  • Version: always 2012-10-17, the current policy language version.
  • Statement: one or more permission rules.
  • Sid: an optional label so humans can tell statements apart.
  • Effect: Allow or Deny.
  • Action: the API calls the rule covers, written as service:Action.
  • Resource: the ARN of what the actions apply to.
  • Condition (optional): extra rules such as source IP, MFA required or a time window.

Why two Resource lines?

Bucket-level actions like s3:ListBucket apply to the bucket ARN. Object-level actions like s3:GetObject apply to the objects inside it, which is why the second ARN ends in /*. Missing one of the two is a very common reason a "correct" policy still gets denied.

What I did hands-on today

  • Created a customer managed policy called ReadDemoBucketOnly using the JSON editor.
  • Created a user group DemoBucketReaders and attached only that policy.
  • Tested it in the Policy Simulator:
    • s3:GetObject on robin-120days-demo/* was Allowed (explicit allow).
    • s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject on the same bucket were Denied (implicit deny).
    • s3:GetObject on a different bucket was Denied, which shows the policy is scoped by resource.

Common mistakes to avoid

  1. "Action": "*" or "Resource": "*" on a statement that doesn't need it.
  2. Forgetting the bucket ARN versus the object ARN (/*).
  3. Copying a policy from the internet without reading every line.
  4. Testing in production first instead of using the Policy Simulator.

3 habits I'm keeping

  1. Start with no permissions and add one action at a time.
  2. Scope the Resource to a specific ARN, not a wildcard.
  3. Test every new policy in the Policy Simulator before attaching it to real users.

Tomorrow (Day 3): IAM roles and how services like EC2 get temporary credentials.

item.title: Building a DevOps Support-Ticket Platform, Part 1: Ubuntu on AWS EC2
item.description: I'm starting a hands-on DevOps project around a support-ticket application. The application will grow through Linux hosting, containers, CI/CD…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
I'm starting a hands-on DevOps project around a support-ticket application. The application will grow through Linux hosting, containers, CI/CD, infrastructure as code, Kubernetes, and recovery exercises.

This first checkpoint is deliberately small: launch an Ubuntu server on AWS, restrict its SSH access, connect to it, and verify the operating system. The ticket application is not deployed yet.

I’m using AI assistance for setup and documentation. My learning rule is to understand each change, check the actual output, and record what has been completed before moving on.

What I launched

Setting Lab configuration
Region Asia Pacific (Mumbai), ap-south-1
Operating system Canonical Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, x86_64
Instance type One t2.micro
Root disk 8 GiB, gp3
Network Default VPC and a public subnet
Public IPv4 Enabled
Login EC2 Instance Connect as ubuntu
Persistent SSH key pair None; browser login uses temporary keys

This is an initial learning configuration. It is not a claim of production readiness or high availability.

The connection path

The browser connects through EC2 Instance Connect to the instance’s SSH service on TCP port 22. Successful access needs both authentication and a working network path.

A public IP alone is not enough. The subnet also needs a route to an internet gateway, the instance needs an SSH service, and the security group must allow the connection source.

Restricting SSH correctly

The launch wizard initially offered SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. That would allow connection attempts from any IPv4 address. I replaced it with the AWS-managed prefix list for EC2 Instance Connect in Mumbai:

com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.ec2-instance-connect

The inbound rule is SSH, TCP 22, with that prefix list as its source. I did not open an application or database port at this checkpoint.

There is an important distinction here:

  • For SSH directly from my laptop, a source of My IP allows my current public IP address.
  • For the browser-based EC2 Instance Connect method used here, the source is AWS’s EC2 Instance Connect service, so its regional prefix list is appropriate.

The security group is only one layer. IAM permissions, temporary SSH authentication, and the instance configuration still matter. Allowing a source in a security group does not by itself authenticate a user.

Why I did not download a PEM file

I chose Proceed without a key pair because this lab uses EC2 Instance Connect. It temporarily provides an SSH public key for authentication, so I did not need a saved private key on my laptop.

This is different from making the machine passwordless or publicly accessible without authentication. If I later want direct SSH access, I will configure that access explicitly.

The first three Linux commands

After connecting, I verified the user, current directory, and distribution:

whoami
pwd
cat /etc/os-release

The relevant output was:

ubuntu
/home/ubuntu
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS"
VERSION_ID="24.04"

whoami confirms which account is executing commands. pwd shows where relative file paths will start. /etc/os-release identifies the distribution and release, which helps choose suitable package-management instructions.

I keep commands separate while learning so it is easy to see which command produced which result.

Cost is part of the lab

A small instance or a Free tier eligible label does not establish that my account has remaining free usage. Account age, plan, credits, and actual consumption affect the bill.

Compute, retained EBS storage, and public IPv4 usage can contribute charges. Closing the terminal does not stop the instance. My end-of-session routine is to save the work, stop the instance from EC2 when it is not needed, and check for resources that remain billable.

What is complete, and what comes next

Completed: one Ubuntu EC2 instance launched, SSH limited to the connection service, browser login successful, and the user, home directory, and OS verified.

Next: refresh package metadata, install the initial tools, create a project workspace, and write a Bash health check. Nginx, the Flask application, persistence, and backups are later checkpoints.

Each checkpoint will have commands, explanations, verification results, and troubleshooting notes committed to the project repository.

Project repository: devops-support-ticket-platform

Official references

  • Get started with Amazon EC2
  • EC2 Instance Connect prerequisites
  • AWS Free Tier FAQs
  • Public IPv4 pricing
  • Stopping and starting EC2 instances

item.title: Salesforce Web-to-Lead & Web-to-Case Cheat Sheet: Forms, Limits, reCAPTCHA and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 24/30)
item.description: Turn website visitors into records without lifting a finger. Web-to-Lead and Web-to-Case come up in almost every admin interview. A generated HTML form…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Turn website visitors into records without lifting a finger. Web-to-Lead and Web-to-Case come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Web-to-Lead HTML form makes leads 500 per day
Web-to-Case HTML form makes cases 5,000 per day
Form Fields Standard plus custom Use the field ID
Protection reCAPTCHA and routing Stop the spam

Interview Q&A

1. What is Web-to-Lead?

A generated HTML form that creates leads from your website.

Tip: No hand coding needed.

2. What are the daily limits?

Web-to-Lead allows 500 a day. Web-to-Case allows 5,000 a day.

Tip: Plan for busy days.

3. How do you add custom fields?

Add the field to the HTML using its field ID.

Tip: Test after adding.

4. What stops spam?

Turn on reCAPTCHA and validate the fields.

Tip: Bots love open forms.

5. How do leads get an owner?

Lead assignment rules route them, or the default owner takes them.

Tip: Rules run automatically.

6. Can customers get a reply?

Yes, auto-response rules email them on creation.

Tip: Keep the template clear.

Scenario Question

"Website enquiries must become leads for sales. How?"

  1. Generate the form in Setup
  2. Add reCAPTCHA and a return URL
  3. Set assignment and auto-response
  4. Test with a sample submit

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Form = generated HTML
  • Lead cap = 500 a day
  • Case cap = 5,000 a day
  • Spam = reCAPTCHA
  • Owner = assignment rule
  • Reply = auto-response

Key Takeaways

  • Generate the form, do not hand build
  • Protect it with reCAPTCHA
  • Route and reply automatically
